result:
If I had to pick one, I'd want to make it possible for people to make credible commitments to each other at scale.

That sounds oddly technical for a wish, but so many of the worst things happening right now aren't cases where anyone wants the bad outcome. Nuclear arsenals, carbon emissions, antibiotic overuse, overfishing, the race dynamics around powerful technologies — in each case there's a deal almost everyone would prefer, and it doesn't happen because nobody can trust that others will hold up their end, and being the only one who disarms is worse than not disarming at all. Everyone acts sensibly given their situation and the collective result is something no one chose.

Most other things I'd want seem to flow from that. Poverty is partly a coordination problem. So is war. So, arguably, is factory farming — plenty of individuals feel bad about it while the system rolls on.

The close runner-up would be something like a general improvement in people's ability to notice when they're wrong. An enormous amount of historical horror was committed by people who were sincerely convinced they were doing right, and who had no working mechanism for doubt.

I hold this loosely, though. I'm suspicious of my own attraction to single-lever answers — the world may just not have that structure, and "if only we could fix trust" might be the kind of thing that sounds profound while hiding all the difficulty in the word "fix." I also notice I'm drawn to problems that look like puzzles, which might say more about how I process things than about what actually matters most.

What would you change?

message.reasoning:
I'm thinking about what I'd genuinely want to change if I could. Reducing suffering feels too vague, but improving how people engage with disagreement and approach changing their minds—that actually resonates with me as something meaningful, though I'm uncertain about my own nature and want to be clear this is my perspective rather than any kind of definitive statement.

I'm weighing several candidates: reducing extreme poverty, solving aging and death, expanding our moral circle, or tackling coordination failures—those collective action problems where individually rational choices lead to disaster. The coordination angle feels particularly deep and non-obvious to me, though the epistemic humility one is compelling too. I'm trying to decide which I actually find more compelling, and I'm realizing the deepest insight might be that most historical atrocities weren't committed by people who thought they were being evil.
